text: For years, security in a software project meant one thing: a team reviewed the application shortly before it shipped, often through a manual assessment. That worked fine when releases happened a few times a year. It breaks down completely when a team ships to production multiple times a day, because there's no longer one convenient moment at the end to gate everything on — and a security team sitting at the very end of the pipeline becomes the thing that makes every release late.

Shifting left means moving security checks earlier on that timeline. Instead of one review at the end, checks run continuously — in the editor as code is written, in a pre-commit hook before anything is even pushed, in the CI pipeline on every pull request, and against a running test deployment before promotion. Security stops being a gate one team owns at the end, and becomes a set of automated checks woven through the same pipeline developers already use every day.

Here's why the timing matters so much. Found in code review, the developer is right there, the context is fresh, and the fix is a small diff before anything is committed — minutes. Found in CI on a pull request, the build fails with a clear annotation and gets fixed before merge. Found in staging, someone has to reproduce it and trace it back through recent commits — hours, and more than one person. Found in production, it's an incident: assessing exploitation, an emergency hotfix, a possible rollback, maybe customer notification.

Every stage adds people, process, and risk the previous stage didn't have. That's the real argument for shifting left — not that production bugs are unfixable, but that fixing them pulls in far more of the organization, far later, with far less room to be wrong. A security step added directly to a pull-request workflow is the simplest version of this in practice, running automatically before a human ever has to get involved.

This chapter builds that out piece by piece. Lesson 22 covers SAST and dependency scanning, which run on every commit before anything deploys. Lesson 23 covers DAST against a running app and container image scanning before deployment — catching a different category of problem entirely. And Lesson 24 tackles the hard part in practice: setting gates that fail builds on real, serious findings without burying every developer in noise they'll learn to ignore.
